Otolaryngology · published research

Dysphonia

Three randomized reports examine PBM for dysphonia. Two pair infrared laser with voice exercise and likely share one cohort; a separate small pilot of PBM alone found no short-term effect.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Behavioral dysphonia and Muscle tension dysphonia categories contain three randomized reports from Brazil. Two 2026 papers report different immediate outcomes from the same 30-woman laser-plus-exercise protocol and likely describe one cohort; a separate 15-person pilot tested PBM alone. These small studies do not establish lasting symptom relief.

Human and clinical evidence

Bacelete et al. randomized 30 women with behavioral dysphonia to active or placebo infrared laser before the voiced tongue-trill technique. Overall voice quality during sustained vowels did not differ significantly between groups. Within-group changes were reported in selected measures, including maximum phonation time, vowel cepstral peak prominence, self-perceived phonatory effort, and vocal-fold vibration; some measures also changed in the placebo-plus-exercise group (Bacelete et al. 2026).

A companion report on the same 30-woman protocol used digital kymography and found an immediate increase in mean opening in the anterior third of the vocal folds. This is a laryngeal-motion measure, not evidence of sustained symptom improvement (Plec et al. 2026).

In a separate 15-person randomized pilot among professional voice users with primary muscle tension dysphonia, PBM alone did not produce immediate or short-term effects on the studied voice outcomes (Pecorari et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the exact dysphonia categories.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The two reports of the 30-woman protocol used an 808 ± 10 nm infrared laser at 100 mW and 1010 mW/cm². It delivered 9 J per point for 1 min 30 s at seven points in one session before the voiced tongue-trill exercise. These parameters describe the combined laser-plus-exercise protocol and should not be attributed to the separate PBM-alone pilot.

Interpretation

The combined protocol produced selected immediate changes, but the reports likely use the same small cohort and overall sustained-vowel voice quality did not differ between groups. The separate PBM-alone pilot was null over short follow-up. Independent trials with patient-centered outcomes and longer follow-up are needed.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for immediate voice changes when PBM is paired with vocal exercise.

Very low for symptom relief or sustained improvement from PBM alone.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two sham-controlled reports use the same 30-woman protocol and likely describe one cohort, leaving one independent study at that size. The separate 15-person PBM-alone pilot found no immediate or short-term benefit. Larger independent studies should separate light from voice therapy and assess lasting, patient-reported outcomes.
